accroche: The book that founded modern linguistics carries a single name on its cover. Its author died without having written a line of it.
contenu_vulgarise:
The *Course in General Linguistics* (*Cours de linguistique générale*) carries a single name on its cover: Ferdinand de Saussure. Translated into dozens of languages and presented for more than a century as the birth certificate of modern linguistics, it is the source of the signifier/signified pair and of the distinctions between *langue* and *parole*, and between synchrony and diachrony. Saussure, however, wrote not one line of it.

## A Book Assembled After the Fact

Between 1906 and 1911, Saussure gave a course in general linguistics three times at the University of Geneva, each time before a small audience. He himself wrote almost no notes with a book in mind: what survives in his hand are scattered drafts with no overall plan. He died on February 22, 1913, at Vufflens-le-Château, without having written the synthesis that would be attributed to him.

His Geneva colleagues Charles Bally and Albert Sechehaye then decided to publish the course anyway. They gathered the notebooks kept by the students who had attended the three sessions (among them Albert Riedlinger), compared versions that were sometimes contradictory, filled in the silences, and organized the whole into a continuous text. The *Course in General Linguistics* was published by Payot in 1916. What generations of students would go on to read as Saussure's thought is, strictly speaking, the reading of it by two men writing in place of a dead man.

## What the Manuscripts Changed

For more than eighty years, this reconstructed text remained the only source. Then, in 1996, renovation work in the orangery of the Saussure family home in Geneva uncovered a box of manuscripts thought lost, including an unfinished sketch titled *On the Dual Essence of Language* (*De l'essence double du langage*). Published in 2002 by Simon Bouquet and Rudolf Engler as *Writings in General Linguistics* (*Écrits de linguistique générale*), these texts show a Saussure more attentive to the role of discourse and of the intersubjective in language than the *Course* would lead one to suppose.

The gap is not just a nuance. According to Bouquet, two of the most-cited notions of the *Course*, the arbitrariness of the sign and linguistic value, become almost incomprehensible, once set against the manuscripts, in the wording Bally and Sechehaye gave them; and the word “discourse,” central in Saussure's drafts, has vanished from the published text. The book that founded structuralism is therefore not quite the one its author had in mind, and it took finding a box in an orangery, by chance, to begin to measure the gap.

repere.texte: Saussure died in 1913 without having written the synthesis attributed to him. Bally and Sechehaye published the Course in General Linguistics in 1916, reconstructed from their students' notebooks. It took until 1996, and the chance discovery of a box of manuscripts in the orangery of the Saussure family home in Geneva, to read pages written in his own hand: published in 2002 as Writings in General Linguistics.
repere.source: Cours de linguistique générale, Payot, 1916; Écrits de linguistique générale, Gallimard, 2002

carte.punch: The founding book of modern linguistics, assembled after his death, never written by Saussure.
carte.idee: The 1916 Course in General Linguistics bears Saussure's signature. He died in 1913 without having written its synthesis, and he owes the text to two colleagues, who recomposed it from student notebooks. Manuscripts found in 1996 reveal a more nuanced thinking than the one published.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The details of the three courses, the history of the edition, and the later philological debates (Godel, Engler, De Mauro).

quiz.question: Why does the 1916 *Course in General Linguistics*, signed Ferdinand de Saussure, pose a particular problem for historians of linguistics?
choix: Because Saussure disowned the text during his lifetime, judging it too far removed from his oral teaching
Because the original manuscript supposedly burned before Bally and Sechehaye could consult it
Because Saussure died before writing it himself; the published text is a reconstruction made by two colleagues from student notebooks
Because it is actually several distinct courses, which linguists have since read as chapters independent of one another
quiz.explication: Saussure died in 1913 without having written the synthesis attributed to him: in 1916, Bally and Sechehaye published a text reconstructed from the notebooks kept by their students. He therefore never had the chance to disown it during his lifetime, and his personal manuscript did not burn: pages in his own hand were, on the contrary, found in 1996, nearly eighty years later. Finally, Bally and Sechehaye's work consisted precisely in unifying three distinct courses into a continuous text, not in placing them side by side as separate chapters.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many times did Saussure teach this course in general linguistics in Geneva?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Between 1906 and 1911, Saussure gave this course three times at the University of Geneva, each time before a small audience, without ever writing the synthesis himself.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Under what circumstances were Saussure's unpublished manuscripts found in 1996?
choix: At an auction of items that had belonged to his family
During renovation work in the orangery of the Saussure family home
While the University of Geneva's archives were being sorted
During the restoration of a municipal library in Vufflens-le-Château
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A box of manuscripts thought lost was uncovered by chance during renovation work in the orangery of the Saussure family home, in Geneva, in 1996.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Simon Bouquet, what do the manuscripts found in 1996 change about how we read the 1916 *Course*?
choix: They show that key notions, such as the arbitrariness of the sign, become almost incomprehensible in the published *Course*
They confirm that Bally and Sechehaye changed nothing in Saussure's text
They show that Saussure had written the entire *Course* himself before his death
They prove that the course was never given orally, only written
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Set against the manuscripts, some of the most-cited notions of the *Course*, such as the arbitrariness of the sign, become almost incomprehensible according to Bouquet, and the word 'discourse,' central to Saussure, has disappeared from the published text.
